segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kama Sutra's ethics chapter let the critics of dharma have their pigeon, and answered with a farmer's seed. Today, the book's very last lines.
screen: `A SEED IN THE GROUND IS REAL TOO.`

segments.voice: Midnight. One more video, then one more, and the thumb seems to be running the show. Somewhere in there a question floats up: who's actually in charge here? The Kama Sutra's last lines take up that question, and they aren't about love at all. They're about the man who wrote the book, and how he says he worked.
screen: `ONE MORE VIDEO.` → `WHO'S IN CHARGE HERE?` → `THE LAST LINES ARE ABOUT THE AUTHOR.`

segments.voice: Vatsyayana says he gathered what older teachers had written, and composed this book while keeping himself restrained, in deep meditation, for the good of the world. Then he says what it is not. It isn't meant, he says, merely as an instrument for satisfying desire. Someone who truly understands it keeps dharma, artha and kama all in view, pays attention to the customs of the people around them, and so gains mastery over the senses. Mastery. That's where a book on pleasure says it's headed. The book's name for the three aims held together is trivarga, the group of three. So the two ends of the book match. The opening sets kama inside the trivarga, beside right living and wealth. The closing says the point of knowing kama is to be master of the senses, not their servant. And mastery here doesn't mean shutting the senses off. A rider doesn't get rid of the horse. The rider holds the reins. The middle of the book, the part it's famous for, this path leaves on the shelf. But the frame says how its author asked the whole to be read: as one part of a life, held by someone still in charge.
screen: `WRITTEN IN RESTRAINT AND MEDITATION.` · `NOT MERELY FOR DESIRE.` · `ALL THREE AIMS IN VIEW.` · then, large: `MASTER OF THE SENSES, NOT THEIR SERVANT.`

segments.voice: If there's something small to eat nearby, a raisin, a square of chocolate, a slice of fruit, hold it and smell it first, and don't eat yet. Notice the pull, and let it be there without obeying it. Then take one slow bite and taste all of it. If there's nothing to eat, do the same with a sip of water.
The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter, closed by the book's last lines: knowing all three aims, and so mastering the senses.
screen: `THE KAMA SUTRA'S ETHICS CHAPTER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Carry this: the Kama Sutra's ethics chapter, not the rest, which ends on mastery of the senses. That closes the book.
